item.subject: Economics
item.question: I'm an HL Economics student (the course first assessed in 2022; my exams are in May 2027). Paper 3 practice, part (a), using the supplied data on Calvessa's steel tariff. A Business Management student will use your answer to analyse a firm that buys steel, so state each result clearly with its units. (i) Calculate the quantity of steel imported by Calvessa before and after the tariff. [2] (ii) Calculate the government's revenue from the tariff. [1] (iii) Calculate the change in the revenue of Calvessa's domestic steel producers. [2] (iv) Calculate the change in the total amount spent on steel by buyers in Calvessa. [2] (v) Calculate the welfare loss resulting from the tariff. [2] (vi) Using a tariff diagram, explain who gains and who loses from the tariff. [3] Write no more than 350 words, plus working and your diagram.

supplied_texts.title: Calvessa steel tariff (data, supplied text)
supplied_texts.author: Task data
supplied_texts.text:
Calvessa: the market for steel (practice data written for this exercise; Calvessa is a fictional country)

Calvessa is a small open economy that can import any quantity of steel at the world price of $600 per tonne. On 1 January 2026 its government imposed a tariff of $150 per tonne on imported steel.

Table 1: The market for steel in Calvessa
Period | Price in Calvessa ($ per tonne) | Domestic quantity supplied (million tonnes per year) | Domestic quantity demanded (million tonnes per year)
Before the tariff (2025) | 600 | 4.0 | 10.0
After the tariff (2026) | 750 | 5.5 | 9.0

Assume that the domestic demand and supply curves are straight lines, and that the world price and all other factors were unchanged between 2025 and 2026.

item.response_text:
All figures are practice data for the fictional economy of Calvessa. I assume, as the data show, that the whole $150 tariff passes into the price paid in Calvessa, so the price rises from $600 to $750 per tonne.

(i) Quantity of steel imported [2]

Formula: imports = domestic quantity demanded − domestic quantity supplied (Table 1)
Before the tariff (2025): 10.0 − 4.0 = 6.0 million tonnes per year
After the tariff (2026): 9.0 − 5.5 = 3.5 million tonnes per year
Imports fall by 2.5 million tonnes per year.

(ii) Government revenue from the tariff [1]

Formula: tariff revenue = tariff per tonne × imports after the tariff
= $150 per tonne × 3.5 million tonnes per year
= $525 million per year

(iii) Change in revenue of domestic steel producers [2]

Formula: revenue = price × domestic quantity supplied
Before: $600 × 4.0 million = $2,400 million per year
After: $750 × 5.5 million = $4,125 million per year
Change = $4,125 million − $2,400 million = +$1,725 million per year (an increase of 71.88%)

(iv) Change in total spending on steel by buyers in Calvessa [2]

Formula: spending = price paid × quantity demanded
Before: $600 × 10.0 million = $6,000 million per year
After: $750 × 9.0 million = $6,750 million per year
Change = +$750 million per year (an increase of 12.5%)

(v) Welfare loss from the tariff [2]

Formula: each welfare-loss triangle = ½ × tariff × horizontal gap
Production triangle (extra domestic output costing more than the world price): ½ × $150 × (5.5 − 4.0) = $112.50 million per year
Consumption triangle (consumption given up): ½ × $150 × (10.0 − 9.0) = $75.00 million per year
Welfare loss = $112.50 + $75.00 = $187.50 million per year

(vi) Who gains and who loses, with a tariff diagram [3]

Diagram 1: Calvessa's market for steel, with a $150 per tonne tariff on imports
Axes: vertical — price of steel ($ per tonne); horizontal — quantity of steel (million tonnes per year)
Curves: D, domestic demand, downward sloping; S, domestic supply, upward sloping; Pw, world supply, horizontal at $600 per tonne; Pw + t, world supply with the tariff, horizontal at $750 per tonne
Change: the tariff raises the import price by $150, so the Pw line moves up to Pw + t (arrow from Pw to Pw + t)
Equilibria: before, price $600, domestic supply 4.0 and domestic demand 10.0 (imports 6.0); after, price $750, domestic supply 5.5 and domestic demand 9.0 (imports 3.5)
Areas: a, producer surplus gain, $712.50 million per year (a rectangle of $600 million on the original 4.0 million tonnes, plus a triangle of $112.50 million on the extra output); b, production triangle, $112.50 million per year; c, tariff revenue, $525 million per year (the rectangle over the 3.5 million tonnes imported); d, consumption triangle, $75 million per year

Domestic steel producers gain. Their revenue rises by $1,725 million per year, but their gain after costs, producer surplus, rises by area a, $712.50 million per year. Revenue is larger because it ignores the cost of the extra output.

The government gains tariff revenue, area c, of $525 million per year.

Consumers lose. They pay $750 instead of $600 per tonne, a rise of 25%, and buy 9.0 instead of 10.0 million tonnes. Their surplus falls by areas a, b, c and d together, $1,425 million per year. A firm that buys steel in Calvessa faces this 25% price rise.

Foreign exporters lose. Imports fall from 6.0 to 3.5 million tonnes, so their sales to Calvessa fall from $3,600 million to $2,100 million per year at the unchanged world price of $600 per tonne, a fall of $1,500 million per year.

Overall, producers and the government gain $1,237.50 million per year in total ($712.50 + $525), which is less than the $1,425 million per year that consumers lose. The difference, $187.50 million per year, is the welfare loss (areas b and d).

Next step: check the totals: consumers' loss ($1,425 million) = producers' gain ($712.50 million) + government revenue ($525 million) + welfare loss ($187.50 million).

Sources: Calvessa steel tariff data (supplied text); general Economics course knowledge (course notes)
